name: Process-based assessment
limitation: Increases instructor workload significantly; students can fabricate a fake process
note: Primary AI-resistant assessment framework; shifts from product evaluation to process evaluation; avoids AI detection tool false positive problems
dinh_nghia: Process-based assessment is an assessment design approach that evaluates students on the demonstrated process of learning and knowledge construction, rather than (or in addition to) the final product submitted. In the context of AI academic integrity, process-based assessment is positioned as the most robust structural approach to AI-resistant assessment because it requires evidence of authentic intellectual work over time — evidence that is difficult for students to fabricate using AI alone. Core mechanisms include: (1) staged submissions (multiple check-ins over an assignment's development); (2) revision history documentation (Google Docs activity tracking, version control); (3) reflective journals (metacognitive commentary on learning); (4) annotated bibliographies that demonstrate the actual research process (not just the sources used). The approach shifts the assessment question from 'what did you produce?' to 'how did you learn?'
phan_loai: Process-based assessment is a prevention method — it restructures the assessment environment rather than detecting violations after the fact. It addresses multiple violation types simultaneously: (1) AI-generated content fraud (the process evidence is hard to AI-generate convincingly); (2) contract cheating (the process evidence requires personal engagement over time); (3) plagiarism (staged submissions reveal if ideas appeared without development). It is distinct from detection tools (Turnitin, GPTZero) and from punitive policies — it reduces the opportunity for fraud rather than punishing it after detection.
lich_su_khai_niem: Process-based assessment has roots in writing pedagogy (process writing approach, Murray 1972; Elbow 1973) and portfolio assessment movements of the 1980s-1990s. It gained new relevance in the academic integrity literature post-2002 (contract cheating rise) and has been revived as the primary AI-resistant assessment strategy post-ChatGPT (2022-present). Key scholarly advocates post-2022: Perkins et al. (2023), Eaton (2024), the Chartered College of Teaching UK (2023 guidance), and the University of Sydney's Learning Futures program. The approach is consistent with constructivist learning theory — it assesses genuine knowledge construction rather than final-product reproduction.
ten_truong_hop: Key adopter institutions: (1) University of Sydney — Learning Futures program; comprehensive assessment redesign including staged submissions, oral components, and process portfolios; explicitly designed as AI-resistant framework (published 2023). (2) University of Wyoming — Prof. Catherine Hartmann's documented use of reflective journals and revision history in writing courses; published case study in academic integrity literature [citation uncertain]. (3) Stanford University — academic integrity policies updated 2023 to include process documentation requirements; Foundation Course assessments redesigned. (4) Chartered College of Teaching UK — 2023 guidance document recommending process-based assessment as primary AI-integrity strategy for UK educators.
dien_bien: Staged submissions: the assignment is broken into checkpoints — topic proposal → outline → first draft → peer review → revised draft → final submission. Each checkpoint is submitted and reviewed; the development trajectory across stages provides evidence of genuine intellectual work. Google Docs revision history: instructors can review the edit history of a shared document, showing when content was added, deleted, or revised. Rapid large text insertions (characteristic of copy-paste from AI tools) are distinguishable from gradual, incremental writing development. Reflective journals: students write metacognitive entries about their learning process — 'what was difficult, what changed my thinking, what I would do differently.' These are highly personal and difficult to AI-generate convincingly. Annotated bibliography: students not only list sources but explain how each source influenced their thinking, showing an authentic research process.
ket_qua_xu_ly: Institutions adopting process-based assessment report: reduced incidence of flagged AI integrity violations (compared to essay-only assessment); greater student engagement with the learning process; improved learning outcomes on measures of genuine comprehension. However, formal comparative studies are limited [uncertain]. The Chartered College of Teaching UK (2023) reported that teachers implementing process-based approaches described increased confidence that assessments reflected genuine student learning. Counterevidence: some students have been documented fabricating revision history (creating multiple document versions artificially to simulate revision), indicating that process documentation alone is not a perfect solution.
con_so_thong_ke: 4 documented adopter institutions (University of Sydney, University of Wyoming, Stanford, Chartered College of Teaching UK) in the task specification; additional adopters include University of California San Diego [uncertain documentation], University of Melbourne [uncertain], and many UK primary/secondary schools through Chartered College guidance. Workload increase for instructors: estimated 30-50% increase in grading time for staged assignments vs. single-submission essays [uncertain specific figure]. False process fabrication rate: not systematically documented [uncertain].
hai_cho_nguoi_hoc: Process-based assessment is the assessment design most aligned with genuine learning outcomes. Students who engage with staged submissions, reflective journals, and annotated bibliographies are doing the intellectual work that education is supposed to develop — even if they also use AI tools for drafting assistance. The approach reduces the 'fake it until you make it' dynamic of final-only assessment, where high AI fraud rates (Springer 2024: 3x self-reported) mean many students are graduating without the competencies their credentials claim.
hai_cho_nghien_cuu: The process-based approach, adapted to research contexts, is consistent with open science practices (pre-registration, analysis plans, documented methodology changes). Requiring graduate students to document their research process (analysis history, draft evolution) has integrity benefits beyond AI fraud prevention — it also reduces fabrication and falsification opportunities.
hai_cho_xa_hoi: If process-based assessment becomes the standard in Vietnamese HE (consistent with QĐ 1705's competency-based education mandate), it would produce graduates whose credentials reflect documented, verified competency development — strengthening the value of Vietnamese degrees in both domestic and international labor markets.
cong_cu_phat_hien: Process-based assessment reduces reliance on post-submission detection tools (Turnitin AI, GPTZero). Google Docs revision history is the most technically robust process-tracking tool: it is built into Google Workspace (widely available in Vietnamese universities through Google for Education programs), produces timestamped activity logs, and is difficult to falsify convincingly. LMS analytics (Moodle, Canvas) can also track submission timing, session length, and activity patterns — providing process evidence without requiring separate document platforms.
han_che_cong_cu: Key limitations: (1) Significant instructor workload increase — reviewing multiple submission stages and revision histories requires substantially more grading time than single-submission assessment; (2) Fabricable process evidence — students can create multiple Google Doc versions rapidly, copy-paste staged to simulate revision, or write generic reflective journal entries without genuine reflection; (3) Scalability challenges — difficult to implement in large lecture courses (200+ students) without significant TA support; (4) Equity concerns — students with competing work/family demands face higher barriers to staged submission timelines; (5) Not applicable to all assessment types — quantitative, laboratory, and performance-based assessments have different process-documentation needs; (6) Requires faculty training and buy-in — significant professional development investment; (7) Privacy concerns with revision history sharing (student consent required in some jurisdictions).
watermarking: Process-based assessment and LLM watermarking are complementary rather than competing approaches. Process documentation could include a watermark verification step: if major LLMs implement production watermarking, instructors could verify that text appearing in a Google Doc in a single large insertion block is watermarked AI output — combining process evidence with watermark detection. In the current absence of production watermarking, process evidence is the most reliable available mechanism.
thiet_ke_bai_tap: Process-based assessment IS the primary 'AI-resistant assessment design' approach. Specific design principles: (1) Break high-stakes summative assessments into low-stakes formative components; (2) Require process artifacts (drafts, outlines, journal entries, annotation) that are inherently personal; (3) Use oral components at the end (brief presentation or discussion of the work) to verify that students understand and can discuss what they submitted; (4) Design reflective prompts that require personal, situated reflection — 'how has this assignment changed your thinking about X?' — rather than generic prompts that AI can answer convincingly; (5) For research assignments, require annotated bibliography entries that explain how each source changed the student's argument, not just what it said.
chinh_sach_truong_hoc: University of Sydney's Learning Futures framework is the most comprehensive institutional implementation — it includes: faculty training workshops, standardized staged submission templates, LMS integration, and student orientation materials explaining the process-based approach. Stanford's 2023 policy update added process documentation requirements to high-risk assessments. The Chartered College of Teaching UK published a practical guide (freely available) for educators implementing process-based approaches in their subject areas.
van_hoa_to_chuc: Process-based assessment is the assessment design approach most consistent with McCabe's honor code culture argument: it builds integrity structurally (by making genuine engagement the path of least resistance) rather than relying on detection and punishment. An institution that invests in process-based assessment is investing in a values-based culture, not an enforcement-first culture. Faculty buy-in is essential — instructors who believe students are fundamentally honest are more likely to implement process-based approaches; instructors who believe enforcement is the primary tool will default to detection tools.
ai_literacy: Process-based assessment is naturally aligned with AI literacy education: stages of the process can include explicit reflection on AI tool use — 'what AI tools did I use, how, and why?' This turns the assessment into a space for developing AI literacy alongside subject-area learning. Students who document their AI use as part of a reflective journal are practicing the kind of critical AI engagement that AI literacy programs aim to develop.
khung_quoc_te: UNESCO 2023 GenAI guidance explicitly recommends process-based and competency demonstration assessment as alternatives to product-only assessment in AI contexts. EU AI Act Article 50 (transparency of AI-generated content) can be operationalized through process documentation requirements. ICAI 6-value framework supports process assessment: the Fairness value requires that assessments give students equitable opportunities to demonstrate genuine learning — process-based assessment more fairly assesses genuine learning than AI-vulnerable product assessments.
phap_luat_viet_nam: QĐ 1705's competency-based education mandate directly supports process-based assessment as the pedagogical model — assessing competency development (not just knowledge output) inherently requires process evidence. Decree 109/2022's fraud prevention mandate can be operationally addressed through process-based assessment, even without explicit legal guidance on AI. Vietnamese universities implementing process-based assessment are fulfilling both documents' intent simultaneously.
chinh_sach_chau_a: NUS (Singapore) has integrated process-based components (including AI use disclosure and process documentation) into its AI Academic Integrity policy (2023/2024). NTU has similar provisions. Japanese universities (Waseda, University of Tokyo) are experimenting with portfolio-based assessment as part of broader curriculum reform. Process-based assessment is consistent with the Confucian educational tradition's emphasis on cultivation (修身) and effort over static assessment of accumulated knowledge.
ai_tutor_vs_ai_cheater: Process-based assessment operationalizes the AI-tutor distinction: if a student can document a genuine learning process that includes AI tool use as one input among many (drafting assistance, feedback, idea generation) alongside personal reflection, revision, and demonstrated understanding, the AI was a tutor — it aided learning. If a student's 'process' shows instant appearance of polished content without development, AI was a substitute — it enabled cheating. The process evidence makes the distinction auditable.
edtech_company_policies: Google Workspace for Education provides revision history at no additional cost — making process documentation infrastructure available to Vietnamese universities on Google's education platform. Moodle (widely used in Vietnamese HE) has assignment submission logging and timeline features that can support staged submissions. Khan Academy's Khanmigo (Socratic AI tutor) is designed to generate process evidence — it records learning interactions, making the AI-tutoring process visible rather than invisible.
de_xuat_nha_nghien_cuu: As an EdTech researcher: (1) Process-based assessment should be the primary recommendation in any Vietnamese HE AI integrity strategy — it is culturally consistent with QĐ 1705, avoids the ESL discrimination problem of detection tools, and directly assesses the competencies Vietnamese education policy values; (2) Propose a national pilot program (funded under QĐ 1705's digital education infrastructure provisions) implementing process-based assessment in 5 universities across different disciplines; (3) Use Google Workspace for Education revision history as the primary process-tracking tool — widely available, free, technically robust; (4) Address the workload limitation by designing assessment schemes where process documentation replaces (not adds to) traditional exam formats; (5) Include process-based assessment as the primary AI literacy module in faculty professional development; (6) Document and publish Vietnamese-context case studies of process-based assessment implementation to build an evidence base for national policy adoption; (7) Acknowledge the fabrication limitation honestly: process-based assessment reduces but does not eliminate AI fraud — it should be combined with occasional oral components for final verification.

nguon_viet_nam: No Vietnamese-language peer-reviewed studies on process-based assessment implementation found [uncertain]. QĐ 1705's competency-based education mandate provides policy alignment. Google for Education partnerships with Vietnamese universities (FPT, VNU) provide the technical infrastructure for revision history tracking. Proposed: HCMUS pilot program using process-based assessment in courses using AI tools.
